`@familiar-ai/core/http` turns a workspace into a [Hono](https://hono.dev) app: JSON commands plus a server-sent event stream for the workspace, each Familiar and each room. Any runtime with the Fetch API can serve it.

## Decide who may do what

`createHttpApi` takes two functions:

- `authenticate(request)` returns the person as `{ id, name }`, or `undefined` for a 401. That person is the author of any message the request posts; a body can't choose its own author.
- `allow(author, operation, resource)` decides whether they may perform the operation. Anything but `true` answers 403. `resource` is `{ familiar }` or `{ room }` from the path, so you can refuse per Familiar or per room.

<Code code={serve} lang="ts" title="api.ts" />

Mount it under any path, such as `new Hono().route('/api', createApi(workspace))`.

Operations are named `group.name`, such as `rooms.post` or `memory.forget`. The `Operation` type is their union, and the [HTTP reference](/familiar/reference/http/) lists each with its route.

Things to know:

- **Allow from a list**, as above, so an operation Familiar adds later is refused until you add it. `allow: () => true` allows everything, now and later; use it only when everyone who can reach the API is the owner, as the daemon does.
- **DMs are private already.** Familiar answers 404 to anyone but a DM's person, whatever `allow` says. Named rooms are open to whoever `allow` lets in.
- **Streams are checked once.** `events.*` operations decide what each stream sends, asked when it connects. Revoking access applies from the next connection.
- **Sign-in streams on `events.account`.** Keep that source to the people who sign the model in.
- **The client offers every command.** One your policy refuses rejects with the 403, so show each person only the UI they may use.

## A Familiar is shared

A Familiar keeps one working context across all its rooms, so what it hears in a DM can come up in a named room, and anything it remembers can reach anyone it replies to. Refusing `events.memory` hides the memory document, not what the model says. Its tools and schedules are shared the same way: anyone allowed to cancel a Familiar's schedules can cancel anyone's.

Give people who mustn't share information [separate workspaces](#one-workspace-per-tenant).

## Identity is not permission

Familiar records who said what. It doesn't decide who may do what. Your host owns:

- authenticating every request, including the event streams
- `allow`, and so each room's audience
- the workspace's tools, and which Familiars use each
- who receives each notification
- which MCP transports, destinations and commands are allowed

Familiar has no per-person tool permissions. When a tool needs narrower rules, such as who may change a task, the tool or the API behind it checks them against `familiar(context).author()`: the person whose message started the call, or the creator of a scheduled run. It comes from storage, never from the tool's arguments, and is `undefined` for background work such as memory filing.

```ts
execute: async ({ taskId }, _api, context) => {
  const author = await familiar(context).author()
  if (!author) {
    return {
      output: [{ type: 'text', text: 'Only a person can do this.' }],
      isError: true,
    }
  }
  // Your API checks, as it runs, whether this person may change the task.
  return updateTask(taskId, { as: author.id })
}
```

MCP tools receive only their arguments, so they can't tell who asked.

Plugins run in your process with its privileges, unsandboxed. The `fetch` Familiar gives them limits where a well-behaved tool sends requests, not what its code can do.

## One workspace per tenant

When your app has separate audiences, such as teams or customers, open one workspace each over that audience's own storage. Choose it from the authenticated session, never from the request. Here each tenant's members share one room with one Familiar:

<Code code={tenants} lang="ts" title="tenants.ts" />

Mount `host.fetch` under your API path, such as with Hono's `app.mount('/api', host.fetch)`. Only one live workspace may own a storage, so a host with several processes routes each tenant to one of them, as a Durable Object does on [Cloudflare](/familiar/build/cloudflare/).

## Notifications

`notify` says what to show and, for a scheduled run, which schedule and who created it. It never chooses recipients. This one delivers through the app's own preferences:

<Code code={notify} lang="ts" title="notify.ts" />

For browser Web Push, pass `push`, a `PushHost`, to `createHttpApi`; without it the `/push` routes answer 404. Its `subscribe` and `unsubscribe` receive the authenticated `Author`. Store each subscription with its subscriber's `id`, and let people remove only their own: an endpoint is no proof of whose browser it is.

## Protect browsers yourself

`createHttpApi` adds no CSRF protection or framing policy. If you authenticate browsers with cookies, add CSRF protection, such as Hono's `csrf` middleware, and set your own `Content-Security-Policy`. It does refuse WebSocket upgrades from another origin.

The daemon is a useful reference for a single-owner host. It authenticates every request as `owner`, listens on loopback, is published only on the owner's tailnet, and adds `csrf`, `frame-ancestors 'none'` and a 30-second push timeout. See [`apps/daemon/src/serve.ts`](https://github.com/AidanZealley/familiar/blob/main/apps/daemon/src/serve.ts).
